paper.title: Can Women Have Children and a Career? IV Evidence from IVF Treatments

evidence.text: Our IV estimates indicate that fertility effects on earnings are: (i) negative, large, and long-lasting; (ii) driven by fertility effects on hourly earnings and not so much on labor supply; and (iii) much stronger at the extensive margin than at the intensive margin.

Equally interesting is our finding that the decline in annual earnings we estimate for having children is far greater than the decline in earnings we get when we estimate the effect of having additional children among women who already have children.

In particular, we sample childless women who go through IVF, treat IVF treatment success at the first IVF treatment as a natural experiment, and subsequently compare the working careers of women after a successful first treatment (treatment group) to those of women after a failed first treatment (comparison group).

We leverage the exogenous timing of sudden and first parental deaths and adopt a matched-control difference-in-differences (DiD) strategy.

paper.title: Effects of Parental Death on Labor Market Outcomes

evidence.text: Women with young children experience a comparatively larger earnings decline (around 4 percent) likely due to the loss of informal childcare.

In contrast, women with young children see a larger earnings drop of almost 4 percent (3.5 percent) after losing their mothers (fathers), while for men with young children, earnings decline by around 1 percent following the death of either parent.
We leverage the exogenous timing of sudden and first parental deaths and adopt a matched-control difference-in-differences (DiD) strategy.
